recommended_title: Six Cheap Statistics versus Worst-Case Bounds: Predicting Random-Walk Cover Times on Small Graphs
central_question: For connected graphs with at most 30 vertices, can a regression on six cheap graph statistics (n, m, mean/max/min degree, diameter) predict the expected cover time more accurately than the classical bounds 2m(n-1) and (4/27)n^3, and how does the error depend on the graph family?
central_thesis: A log-linear ridge regression on six cheap statistics, fitted on Monte Carlo labels, predicts held-out isomorphism-disjoint small-graph cover times with mean absolute log error 0.183 (95% CI 0.167-0.207) against 1.397 for the better of the two generic bounds. Its advantage is significant in 9 of 10 families, is largest where the bounds are loosest (complete, Erdos-Renyi, random 3-regular), and is not statistically clear on the lollipop family, where the cubic bound is nearly tight; the predictor's own residual error is highest on complete, grid and Erdos-Renyi graphs.
narrative_rationale: The only sealed final evidence is a completed, qualified evaluation of one predictor (the frozen selection, which is the original log-linear ridge configuration; the search produced no qualifying improved variant). That evidence answers the task's two questions directly: (i) accuracy against generic bounds, with paired two-level bootstrap CIs at plane and family level, and (ii) per-family reliability and failure. The bound-slack-by-family pattern gives a mechanistic reading: worst-case bounds are tight only near their extremal families (lollipop, path), so a fitted predictor gains most where the true cover time is far from the worst case. Evaluator controls (permuted-feature predictions, reordered-copy invariance, isomorphism-disjoint splits, closed-form simulator checks) let the paper make calibrated claims. A method-novelty story is unsupported, and so is a search-improvement story, because no new variant was scored. A pure negative-results story would misrepresent a qualified, strongly positive measurement. The strongest honest frame is therefore an empirical characterization study: a simple, reproducible predictor, controlled comparisons, and a family-resolved map of where it is reliable and where it is not.

method_groups.name: Statistics-only log-linear ridge predictor (studied method)
method_groups.include_reason: This is the frozen, sealed-evaluated predictor. It regresses ln(cover time) on the logs of the six statistics plus a ln n * ln diameter interaction, standardized, with ridge 1e-3 and an unpenalized intercept. Present it as a simple reproducible predictor, not a novel architecture.

method_groups.name: Generic analytic upper bounds used as predictors: 2m(n-1), (4/27)n^3, and their pointwise minimum
method_groups.include_reason: These are the task's named comparator and the main answer to the research question. The pointwise minimum ('best bound') is the strongest bound-based predictor. Its paired plane-level and per-family delta CIs exist.

method_groups.name: Matthews-type reference: exact maximum hitting time x H_{n-1}
method_groups.include_reason: This reference is a much tighter bound but needs the full graph, not cheap statistics. It shows the statistics-only predictor beats even a graph-aware bound on average (point estimates only; no paired CI is available).

method_groups.name: Fitted reference predictors: OLS on (ln n, ln m) and a constant (geometric-mean training label)
method_groups.include_reason: The OLS(ln n, ln m) reference isolates the value of the degree and diameter statistics beyond size alone (paired delta CI available). The constant sets a floor for what fitting without features achieves. Neither is a training-matched ablation of the studied predictor; describe both as evaluator reference predictors.

method_groups.name: Permuted-feature control
method_groups.include_reason: The same fitted predictor is applied to deranged feature rows. The error rises to 1.261 (paired delta CI 0.955-1.196), showing that the predictions depend on each graph's own statistics.

results_focus: Plane-level accuracy: predictor 0.183 [0.167, 0.207] mean absolute log error vs best bound 1.397, Feige leading term 1.604, AKLLR 1.836, Matthews reference 0.605, OLS(ln n, ln m) 0.526, constant 0.942. Paired delta vs best bound CI [-1.303, -1.130]; paired delta vs OLS CI [-0.391, -0.288].

Per-family reliability map: predictor error ranges from 0.056 (star) to 0.381 (Erdos-Renyi). Low-error families are star, random 3-regular, random tree and path (<=0.1). Highest error is on complete 0.357, grid 0.364 and Erdos-Renyi 0.381.

Per-family paired gain over best bound: largest on random 3-regular (-2.09), complete (-2.08) and Erdos-Renyi (-2.07). It is significant in 9 of 10 families. Lollipop: -0.111, CI [-0.225, 0.013], which includes zero.

Mechanistic reading via bound slack (best-bound error = predictor error minus delta, derived per family): slack is smallest on lollipop (~0.28) and path (~0.48), the families near the bounds' worst case, and largest on complete/Erdos-Renyi (~2.4). Gains track slack.

Validity and uncertainty: permuted-feature control, order invariance 0, isomorphism overlap 0, no capped walks, median Monte Carlo relative SE 0.033, two-level bootstrap (graphs within family plus walks). Seed range 0 reflects a deterministic predictor on fixed labels, not robustness across data draws.
Limits on statistics-only prediction: 12 held-out graphs share their exact six-statistic vector with another graph, so any statistics-only predictor must give them identical predictions.
figure_plan: Fig. 1 (page 1-2, full width): a concept overview. Ten synthetic graph families give a six-statistic vector. A log-linear ridge model produces a predicted cover time, set beside the two generic bounds. The evaluation side shows Monte Carlo labels, isomorphism-disjoint held-out graphs and paired bootstrap.

Fig. 2 (full width, 2 panels): per-family reliability map. (a) Dot plot of the predictor's mean absolute log error and the best bound's error per family, families sorted by bound slack. (b) Paired delta vs best bound with 95% bootstrap CI and a zero line, so the lollipop interval crossing zero is visible.

Fig. 3 (full width or ~0.8 textwidth, 2 panels): plane-level comparison. (a) Fitted/statistics predictors: studied predictor with CI, OLS(ln n, ln m), constant, permuted-feature control. (b) Bound-based predictors: best bound, (4/27)n^3, 2m(n-1), Matthews reference.
Table 1: plane-level errors and paired-delta CIs for every comparator. Table 2: the family roster with held-out counts derived from the evaluator catalogue.

figure_specs.purpose: Show the problem, the predictor and the evaluation protocol at a glance: graph families -> six cheap statistics -> log-linear ridge -> predicted cover time vs generic bounds, scored on isomorphism-disjoint held-out graphs with Monte Carlo labels and paired bootstrap.
figure_specs.layout_rationale: The ICLR template is single column with a 5.5 in text width. A left-to-right pipeline with small graph-family glyphs needs the full width so stage labels stay at or above 8 pt. Place it at the top of page 2, or page 1 if space allows.

figure_specs.purpose: Answer the second research question: the predictor's error per graph family next to the best bound's error, plus the paired gain with 95% bootstrap CI. This shows where the predictor is reliable and where its advantage vanishes (lollipop).
figure_specs.metric: mean absolute log error; paired delta vs best bound with 95% CI
figure_specs.split_by: panel: (a) error per predictor, (b) paired delta
figure_specs.layout_rationale: Ten family rows with horizontal dots read best at the full 5.5 in width with two side-by-side panels sharing the family axis (about 5.5 x 3.0 in). Use a log-scale x-axis in panel (a) because errors span 0.06-2.45. Do not shrink: keep tick labels >= 8 pt.

figure_specs.purpose: Compare overall accuracy of the studied predictor against fitted references, the permuted-feature control and bound-based predictors.
figure_specs.metric: family-weighted mean absolute log error (CI only where available: studied predictor)
figure_specs.split_by: panel: (a) fitted / control predictors, (b) bound-based predictors
figure_specs.layout_rationale: Two panels of four bars each with long predictor names need horizontal bars. At about 0.85 text width (about 4.7 x 2.2 in) labels stay legible, and a shared x-axis range lets the reader compare panels. Table 1 carries the exact values, so the figure stays sparse.

supplementary_plan.purpose: Provide full reproducibility detail, the complete per-family metric table with all paired CIs, exact definitions of the predictor and comparators, the validity diagnostics, the search-versus-final scope note with the unscored-attempt disclosure, and the required LLM Usage statement. Nothing essential to the thesis is moved out of the main text.

planned_subsections.heading: Full Per-Family Results
planned_subsections.grounded_content: A table with all ten families: predictor error, derived best-bound error, paired delta and its 95% CI. Note that per-family CIs for the predictor's own error are not reported by the evaluator.

planned_subsections.heading: Evaluation Protocol and Validity Diagnostics
planned_subsections.grounded_content: Graph generation and splits (deterministic catalogue split by n mod 3; random families resampled until isomorphism-disjoint; about 117 training and 116 held-out graphs, derived from the evaluator). Monte Carlo labels with 256 walks per graph and a step cap. Closed-form simulator checks. The paired two-level bootstrap with 1000 replicates. Diagnostics: iso overlap 0, order invariance 0, capped walks 0, failed episodes 0, median MC relative SE, feature-collision count 12.

planned_subsections.heading: Reproducibility: Environment, Commands and Seeds
planned_subsections.grounded_content: Predictor source summary (design matrix, standardization, ridge 1e-3, clipping and fallback). Episode reset seeds 211/212/213 and identical per-episode errors. Evaluator plane seeds from the final plane configuration. CPU-only runtime of roughly 0.6-1.2 s per episode.

notes_for_writer: Body budget (venue hard constraint): 8-9 pages of body, with the final body page at least 75% full. The task brief permits a short paper but does not cap length, so follow the venue. Spend the space on (1) a precise problem definition and cover-time background, (2) the reasoning behind the features and the log target, (3) the evaluation protocol and controls, (4) the per-family analysis with the bound-slack reading, and (5) a substantive limitations section. Do not pad.

Suggested body layout: Introduction with 3 verifiable contributions (~1.2 pp); Background: cover time and generic bounds (~0.7 pp); Predictor (~0.9 pp); Evaluation protocol, with Table 2 (~1.2 pp); Results: Table 1, Fig. 3, Fig. 2, controls (~2.3 pp); Discussion: where cheap statistics suffice and why bounds are loose (~0.8 pp); Limitations (~0.6 pp); Conclusion (~0.3 pp). Place Fig. 1 on page 1-2.

Frame the contribution as an empirical characterization with controlled comparisons, not a new method. The predictor is a deliberately simple log-linear ridge regression. Its value is accuracy relative to bounds plus the family-resolved reliability map.

State clearly that bounds are guarantees while the predictor is fitted on in-distribution labels and guarantees nothing. The comparison treats the bounds as predictors, as the task defines it. Never call the predictor a bound.

Metric wording: 'mean absolute log error' (|ln pred - ln C| capped at ln 1000), averaged within family and then equally across ten families. You may translate 0.183 to a geometric-mean multiplicative error of about exp(0.183) ≈ 1.20 and 1.397 to about 4.0. Say 'geometric-mean ratio', not 'percent error'.

Qualification: the sealed final evaluation completed with outcome 'qualified' (final.qualification.*). Report the validity checks that back it: isomorphism-disjoint held-out graphs (overlap 0), order invariance (0), no capped walks, no failed episodes, closed-form simulator checks. Do not use pipeline labels for this; describe the checks themselves.

Uncertainty: report the plane CI [0.167, 0.207] and the paired-delta CIs. The three evaluation episodes (seeds 211-213) give identical errors (seed range 0) because the predictor is deterministic and labels are fixed. Say explicitly that this is not variability across data draws; all uncertainty comes from the two-level bootstrap. The median Monte Carlo relative SE of the labels is 0.033.

Lollipop: the paired delta CI [-0.225, 0.013] includes zero. Write 'no statistically clear advantage', not 'worse'. Interpret it through bound tightness: lollipop graphs are the extremal family for the cubic bound (state this as background, with a citation only if the bib supports it).

Per-family best-bound errors are derived as predictor error minus delta. Label them 'derived' in figure captions and tables. Per-family CIs for the predictor's own error are not reported, so use the delta CIs only.

High-error families (complete 0.357, grid 0.364, Erdos-Renyi 0.381): any explanation, such as a different growth regime that one log-linear surface cannot capture, or few training graphs per deterministic family, must be labelled a hypothesis. No ablation tests it.

OLS(ln n, ln m) reference: it is evaluator-defined and differs from the studied predictor mainly in the feature set. Call it a size-only reference that indicates the value of the degree and diameter statistics, not a controlled ablation of the studied predictor.

Matthews reference (0.605) needs exact hitting times from the full adjacency, so it is not a cheap statistic. Only point estimates exist, with no paired CI. Avoid significance language for this comparison.

Feature collisions: 12 held-out graphs share an exact six-statistic vector with another graph. This is an inherent ambiguity for statistics-only predictors. Which families are affected is not reported, so do not guess.

Selection scope: no improved variant was scored (1 attempt, 0 scored, 1 unscored). Disclose this briefly, in the supplement plus one sentence in limitations, as missing evidence and not a loss. Never describe the unscored variant's design as if it was evaluated, and never claim an improvement over a baseline: the studied predictor is the original configuration.

Scope of claims: ten synthetic families, 5 <= n <= 30, uniform-start expected cover time, training and test drawn from the same families. Do not claim transfer to unseen families, larger n or real-world graphs.

Citations: references.bib currently has only the Lovasz survey (use key Lovász2001RandomWO; avoid the garbled duplicate Asz1993RandomWO) and Aleliunas et al. 1979. Feige's cubic bound and the Matthews bound have no bib entries. Unless the writing stage adds verified entries, attribute them by name in prose without inventing BibTeX. Do not search for or cite the original paper answering this research question, or pages that discuss it.

Figures: generate from paper_data.json values with matplotlib. Export PDF plus a 300-DPI PNG, include the PDF in LaTeX, and use one consistent color for the studied predictor and another for the bounds across Fig. 2 and Fig. 3. The figure directory is currently empty, so every figure must be generated. For Fig. 1, use generate-concept-figure; if it fails, fall back to TikZ and note why.

Table 2 (family roster) counts come from the evaluator's deterministic catalogue and per-family random counts: 9 each for path, cycle, star, complete and binary tree; 5 grid; 18 lollipop; 16 each for random tree, Erdos-Renyi and random 3-regular, giving 116 held-out graphs. Describe these as protocol facts from the evaluator source, not as metrics.
Venue: double-blind. No names, links or acknowledgements. Include an 'LLM Usage' section, which may go in the appendix.
